text:
ISSUES REGARDING workplace bullying are again in the news in Taiwan. Specifically, the death of deputy trade representative Yen Huai-hsing in March at age 53, one month after her resignation in February, led to increased scrutiny on trade representative Yang Jen-ni. After Yen’s death, reports emerged that Yang bullied Yen.

As a result, President Lai Ching-te has now dismissed Yang. Yang has affirmed her innocence, suggesting that she may take legal action over the damage to her reputation.

This was not the first time that the death of a public servant led to a discussion about issues involving workplace bullying. In November 2024, a 39-year-old public servant surnamed Wu was found dead in the Xinzhuang Joint Office Tower in New Taipei due to an apparent suicide.

Wu’s suicide was thought to be due to workplace bullying, as well as the weight of responsibilities for being the only staff member who performed employment information services. Wu was under significant pressure over being responsible for creating an employment services system.

Wu’s superiors later faced demotions, with Hsieh Yi-jung being dismissed as head of the northern regional office of the Work Development Agency. Minister of Labor Ho Pei-shan stepped down to take responsibility for the matter, having drawn flak for previously stating that she did not have the authority to immediately dismiss Hsieh. After Ho’s resignation, current Minister of Labor Hung Sun-han took up the position.

After the most recent controversy about workplace bullying, new guidelines were rolled out to address the issue. Workplace bullying is defined as “inappropriate words or behaviors” that are “beyond the necessary and reasonable business scope” and cause physical or mental harm to workers, as caused by the repeated actions of personnel at a business entity.

The workplace regulations set specific timelines for conducting reports and taking action regarding incidents of workplace bullying, with differing regulations for companies of different sizes. At the same time, employers are still the ones to whom incidents of workplace bullying are to be reported. It may be the case that employers do not act on reports or do not notify the Ministry of Labor about them, or that employers are themselves the source of workplace bullying.

The changes apply across the board, including not only Taiwanese, but also white-collar and blue-collar non-Taiwanese workers, better known as migrant workers. Taiwanese civil society groups that work on issues involving migrant labor, however, have suggested that the implementation of anti-bullying measures for migrant workers will probably be lacking. It is also likely that migrant workers may not be in the same position as Taiwanese workers in terms of legal recourse when it comes to bullying, given the systematic discrimination against them that is institutionalized in the blue-collar migrant work system.

Brian Hioe is one of the founding editors of New Bloom. He is a freelance journalist, as well as a translator. A New York native and Taiwanese-American, he has an MA in East Asian Languages and Cultures from Columbia University and graduated from New York University with majors in History, East Asian Studies, and English Literature. He was Democracy and Human Rights Service Fellow at the Taiwan Foundation for Democracy from 2017 to 2018 and is currently a Non-Resident Fellow at the University of Nottingham's Taiwan Studies Programme, as well as board member of the Taiwan Foreign Correspondents' Club.
